questions.q: What is the most fundamental difference between Qiskit and Q#?
options: Qiskit only supports simulators, while Q# only supports real hardware
Qiskit cannot represent entanglement, while Q# can
Qiskit is a Python SDK (quantum objects inside a classical language), while Q# is its own standalone, compiled, statically-typed language
Q# is slower than Qiskit because it is interpreted rather than compiled
questions.explain: Qiskit circuits are Python objects built with ordinary Python code; Q# is a separate domain-specific language with its own grammar and compiler (the QDK), where operations, types, and control flow are language constructs, not library calls.

questions.q: In Q#, what does it mean for an operation to be a 'first-class citizen'?
options: Operations run faster than functions because they are compiled to machine code
Operations are stored in a special cloud database managed by Azure Quantum
Operations can only be called once per program
Operations are declared, typed constructs the compiler checks directly, and the compiler can derive transformations like Controlled or Adjoint automatically from an operation's own definition
questions.explain: Because operations are a core language construct with declared signatures, Q#'s compiler can automatically generate a controlled or adjoint (inverse) version of an operation without the developer writing a second implementation by hand.

questions.q: What does the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator actually produce, and how does it produce it?
options: A cost estimate in US dollars for renting Azure cloud VMs to run the simulation
A report of physical/logical qubit counts and estimated runtime for a Q# program against a stated hardware profile, computed without running the program on any real or simulated device
A list of syntax errors in the Q# program, similar to a linter
A live benchmark of the program's actual runtime on a real quantum computer in Azure's data centers
questions.explain: The resource estimator analyzes a Q# operation against an error budget and hardware assumptions to estimate qubit counts and runtime for future fault-tolerant hardware -- it does not execute the program on any device, simulated or real.

questions.q: A team needs to wire a quantum subroutine into an existing Python/pandas data pipeline with minimal integration friction, with no need for pre-fault-tolerant hardware estimates. Which choice fits best, and why?
options: Azure Quantum Resource Estimator, because it is the only tool that can call pandas
Qiskit, because it's Python-native and the quantum code runs in the same runtime as the rest of the pipeline with no serialization boundary
Neither -- quantum code cannot be combined with classical Python pipelines
Q# standalone .qs project, because static typing is required for pandas interoperability
questions.explain: When the priority is tight integration with an existing Python-based classical workflow and resource estimation isn't the goal, Qiskit's Python-native ecosystem avoids any serialization/interop boundary that a separate compiled language would introduce.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between Q# and Python in practice?
options: Q# is a superset of Python syntax, so any valid Python file is also a valid Q# file
Q# code must always be manually rewritten into Qiskit before it can be used in any Python workflow
They are not mutually exclusive -- the `qsharp` Python package lets Python/Jupyter workflows call into Q# operations, bridging the two ecosystems
Python cannot call Q# under any circumstances; they are fully isolated runtimes
questions.explain: The `qsharp` Python package (used later in this course) allows Q# operations to be compiled and invoked from Python/Jupyter, making it practical to combine Q#'s strengths with an existing Python-based workflow rather than forcing an either/or choice.
